## 2.1. Data Rescue Program

  Between 2024 and 2025, DFO and the CIEE Living Data Project undertook a data-rescue initiative to recover, standardize, quality-control, and archive historical acoustic-trawl survey (ATS) datasets collected between 1977 and 2007.  The DFO staff involved in the data-rescue initiative were not part of DFO’s ATS field crews that collected the data. Therefore, in cases where documentation was incomplete, data-processing decisions were informed by file structure, historical reports, metadata, and consultation with DFO staff familiar with ATS operations. Data rescue activities were completed using R and RStudio [@base], and all scripts and outputs are available through the Open Data repository.

  The data collected by LEP were saved into annual proprietary data files titled *TARGETyy.dat* (for acoustic) and *TRAWLyy.dat* (for trawl), where *yy* indicates a two-digit value representing ATS sampling year. In some years, these data were supplemented from data saved in SAS binary format (.sas7bdat extension; *e.g.*, TRAWLyy.sas7bdat for files including fish data, and TRLINFyy.sas7bdat files for analogous survey meta-data). 

  ATS years span 1 April through 31 March of the following calendar year, corresponding approximately to a single juvenile Sockeye Salmon cohort, *i.e.* from 01-Apr-yy to 31-Mar-yy+1. Some juvenile Sockeye Salmon (age-1+) stay an extra year in the lake and leave as smolts the following year before the end of March. Trawl biosampling data after 1999, and acoustic target data after 2007, as well as occasional records within this timeframe that may have been missed, may be available in Excel files or scanned field notes held by the SiRE Program at Fisheries and Oceans Canada, but have not been extracted as part of the current data recovery and cleaning process.

### 2.1.1. Acoustic Target Data Rescue

  The acoustic target data were obtained from ASCII data files (*i.e.*, text files with suffix .dat) generated by a PASCAL program (Pop-P, written in-house). These data were originally collected using hydroacoustic counts from echo-sounders of “fish-like-targets” (FLT) from 1977 to 2007. From 2000 to 2007, trawl sampling data were unavailable for recovery as SAS7BDAT or DAT files; consequently, the acoustic data rescued here for this period lacks corresponding comprehensive species composition records. However, the relative proportions of Sockeye and Stickleback – ascertained by researchers based on the original but now-unavailable trawl data – are recorded as part of the acoustic records’ metadata. The acoustic data in TARGETyy.dat files were organized by ATS year, with text blocks specific to each lake and survey date. The text blocks consist of a header block of meta-data (lake code, date, sounder type, etc.) for each survey, followed by individual records for FLT values for each transect and depth level. Sockeye Salmon and Stickleback species proportions – ascertained by researchers based on trawl data – were appended to each record.
 
  The data cleaning process for the acoustics data is explained in detail in the "Data Cleaning" section of the "DFO-LEP Acoustic Target Data Issues (1977-2007).pdf" file in the "output" folder [@zotero-item-913]. Briefly, a script (`Acoustic Target Data Cleanup.R`) was developed to compile and clean the .dat data files using R version 4.3.1 and RStudio 2024.09.1 Build, 394[^02-methods-5]. The script imported raw data from .dat files, perform data cleaning, such as duplicates analysis, and compilation into integrated .csv output files. Output files were timestamped, and an additional annotated file with comments regarding any data issues encountered was created. All files, including a data dictionary describing all variables of the dataset, are available for downloading from the Open Data Repository [@zotero-item-913]. The acoustic target data were incorporated into the final data compilation of both acoustic and trawl records, *FINAL_xxdays_match_trawl_and_acoustic.csv* (where xx represents the interval, in days), which is available from https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/5b5d3312-12e6-4265-b07b-c69dcc17a566.
  
[^02-methods-5]: The pipeline uses the following R packages: tidyverse [@tidyverse], progress [@progress], tictoc [@tictoc], tibble [@mullerTibbleSimpleData2016], and base R Tools.

### 2.1.2. Trawl Biosample Data Rescue

  The original trawl biosample data were also ASCII data files (.dat) organized by ATS year, containing multiple lake systems and multiple trawls per lake. Fish measurements were originally collected using an Apple computer-based electronic caliper system and subsequently incorporated into annual trawl data files. Each lake/trawl data block consisted of a header block of trawl meta-data (*e.g.*, lake code, date, net-size, species code, etc.), followed by specimen information (fish length, weight and scale book number/letter) for each individual fish sample. A total of 22 files, spanning 1977 to 1999, were available to extract trawl data from. 

  An R (version 4.5.2) script was created to loop over the .dat files to extract trawl information, facilitated by RStudio 2025.09.2 Build 418. Each loop used the total number of fish collected per trawl event to determine how many rows to create. The trawl-level metadata were repeated for each specimen, while the specimen-specific information, such as length and weight, was recorded separately for each fish. The .dat files did not have header names as part of the data; these were added when the data were read into R[^02-methods-6]. The line number of each record was extracted from the .dat file and included in the final table, as well as the name of their source file to increase traceability. In some of the .dat files, the original processor included comments related to the trawl event in the metadata block. These comments, once included in an interim comma-delimited file, were extracted from the main data columns using the stringr package and transferred to a separated column, linked to the name of the original field they were assigned to. The dates and times were standardized following the international ISO 8601 format. The lake names, preservative and species names were added to the table by joining their corresponding codes to lookup tables originally created by DFO personnel. A cleaned table was created for each ATS year and saved separately as .csv. Six scripts were created to address the nuances in the data files.

[^02-methods-6]: All cleaning steps were completed using a combination of base R and the tidyverse package and its associated packages: dplyr, lubridate, stringr and tidyr.

  For 1977-1983, surviving DAT files were available only as tabular exports that lacked documentation and omitted portions of the original record structure (Appendix A). Consequently, these files were not used directly for data recovery. Instead, data for these years were primarily recovered from corresponding SAS7BDAT datasets that had been constructed from the original data.

  Data in SAS7BDAT-format files (1977-1999) were read using the haven package [@wickhamHavenImportExport2015]. These SAS7BDAT files were originally derived from the tabulated .dat files, which are no longer available in that format. From 1983 to 1999, both file formats were available and where there were conflicts between the two, the .dat values were used. All 22 SAS7BDAT files available, which spanned from 1977 to 1999, were used to extract trawl data. As the data were already tabulated, the cleaning process involved renaming the columns to standardize them and joining the corresponding codes to lookup tables. Duplicate rows were screened and removed, and the dates and times were also standardized following the international ISO 8601 format. One script was created to loop over all .sas7bdat files and create final, cleaned tables separated by ATS year and saved as comma-delimited .csv text files.

  Unique identifiers were generated for both trawl events and individual fish records using combinations of date, lake, trawl number, sampling depth, species codes, and biological measurements. These codes facilitated duplicate detection and merging of source tables.
  
### 2.1.3. Quality Control of Trawl Biosample Data

  The final dataset, *Trawl_data_FINAL_1977-1999.csv*, was created by merging from all recovered sources. First, when applicable, the ATS year tables were merged the R package joyn [@joyn], as it keeps all columns and rows from both tables. Next, a function was created to reconcile duplicate records (*i.e.*, rows with the identical fish unique identifier), and in case of conflict (*i.e.*, different values in records with the same identifier), values from the original .dat files supersede data from .sas7bdat files. Merge outcomes and subsequent data modifications were documented using record-level quality-control flags (see *Data_dictionary_final_dataset* for details).
  
  Quality-control procedures included:
1. verification and recalculation of trawl end times and duration;
2. recalculation of standardized fish weights based on preservative type;
3. identification and correction of unit inconsistencies (*e.g.*, cm vs. mm; g vs. mg);
4. screening of length and weight outliers using the condition factor (K); and
5. standardization of fields and formats across all source datasets.
  All modified records were flagged in the *data_issues* field to maintain traceability. Condition factor (K) was calculated using standardized fish length (cm) and weight (g) according to the formula below.  

\begin{equation}
  K = 100 \times \frac{W}{L^3}
  (\#eq:kindex-eq)
\end{equation}

## 2.2. Data Visualization {#sec:math}

  This report was created using R Markdown [@rmarkdown2025][^02-methods-7]. Tables and figures were generated using R, with ggplot2 used for data visualization [@wickhamGgplot2CreateElegant2007; @wickhamGgplot2ElegantGraphics2016]. A viridis colour palette was selected to improve accessibility for readers with colour-vision deficiencies. Throughout the report, darker colours represent acoustic-target data and yellow colours represent trawl-biosample data. To simplify visualization, analyses focusing on individual lakes were restricted to the 16 most frequently surveyed lakes. The lakes included as key lakes are: Cheewhat Lake, Great Central Lake, Henderson Lake, Hobiton Lake, Kennedy Lake, Long Lake, Meziadin Lake, Muriel Lake, Nimpkish Lake, Owikeno Lake, Skidegate Lake, Sproat Lake, Tahltan Lake, Vernon Lake, Woss Lake, and Yakoun Lake.

[^02-methods-7]: Facilitated by the packages csasdown 0.0.0.90034 [@csasdown] and flextable [@flextable]. R package citations were created using the package grateful [@grateful].

  Summary figures were generated to describe the temporal, spatial, and biological characteristics of the rescued ATS datasets. Visualizations were intended to support data exploration and provide users with an overview of survey effort, dataset coverage, fish abundance metrics, species composition, and biological characteristics across lakes and ATS years.
  
  Survey effort was summarized using the number of survey dates, trip frequencies, and lake coverage through time. Acoustic-target data were visualized using distributions of surveyed depth ranges, fish-like target (FLT) abundance estimates, and observer-derived species composition information. Trawl biosampling data were summarized using species composition, fish length and weight distributions, length-weight relationships, and other biological characteristics.
  
  To facilitate interpretation of long-term patterns, detailed lake-specific visualizations were limited to the 16 most frequently surveyed waterbodies ("key lakes"). Unless otherwise stated, annual summaries were calculated from all available surveys within an ATS year. Figures are intended to describe dataset characteristics and data availability rather than to provide formal trend analyses or statistical inference.
  
  Species-composition summaries were derived from trawl biosampling records by calculating the proportion of fish identified as Sockeye Salmon within each trawl event[^02-methods-8]. Annual lake-specific Sockeye Salmon proportions were then calculated as weighted means, with weights proportional to the number of fish captured in each trawl. Weighting was applied to reduce the influence of small catches and to better represent the relative contribution of individual trawl samples to annual species-composition estimates. 
  
  Because species identities are not directly observed in hydroacoustic surveys, annual Sockeye Salmon proportions derived from trawl biosamples may differ from observer-assigned species proportions recorded within acoustic source files. Both summaries are presented to facilitate comparison between the rescued trawl dataset and historical acoustic records.

[^02-methods-8]: Only trawl samples containing at least one identified fish were included in species-composition calculations.

Length-weight relationships were estimated separately for four species (Sockeye, Coho, Chinook and Stickleback) using linear regression of log-transformed weight and length data, where *W* is fish weight (g), *L* is fish length (mm), *a* is the intercept (scaling constant), and *b* is the allometric growth coefficient. Model fit was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (*R²*).

  $$W = aL^b$$
  $$ln(W) = ln(a) + bln(L) + \epsilon$$
